source_text: Dicit nos mortuos esse peccato eo iam tempore, quo, ut acciperemus indulgentiae donum, renuntiare nos mundo omnibusque peccatis professi sumus, atque ideo muneris memores debere sic vivere, ut Christo consepulti esse doceamur atque resurrectionem eius conspicua sanctitate gestemus et, quomodo ille, postquam resurrexit a mortuis, nullas infirmitates corporis, nulla flagella perpetitur, ita etiam et nos esse invulnerabiles peccatis omnibus et vitiis annitamur. Si enim complantati sumus similitudini mortis eius, simul et resurrectionis erimus hoc scientes, quoniam vetus homo noster simul confixus est cruci, ut destruatur corpus peccati, ut ultra non serviamus peccato; qui enim mortuus est, iustificatus est a peccato [n374] . Clara fideles ratione constringit; si vultis, inquit, resurrectionis eius fieri participes, virtutem quoque mortis imitamini, ut mortui vitiis in virtute vivatis; tunc enim eritis in illa felicitate consortes, si mortis eius imaginem tuleritis moriendo peccatis; vetus enim homo noster debet cruci eius affixus doceri, ut destruat corpus peccati fortitudine videlicet passionis. Corpus autem peccati consuetudine sua Paulus vitia, non substantiam carnis appellat; sic enim sequitur: Ut destruatur corpus peccati, ut ultra non serviamus peccato; qui enim mortuus est, iustificatus est a peccato.
pass_a_gloss: He says that we have died to sin already at that time at which, so that we might receive a gift of indulgence, we professed that we renounce the world and all sins, and therefore mindful of the gift we ought so to live that we may be taught to have been buried together with Christ and may carry his resurrection by a conspicuous holiness and, as he, after he rose from the dead, suffers no infirmities of the body, no scourges, so also even we may strive to be invulnerable to all sins and vices. For if we have been planted together to the likeness of his death, we shall be also of the resurrection, knowing this, that our old human being has been fixed together to the cross, so that the body of sin may be destroyed, so that we may no longer serve sin; for he who has died has been justified from sin. He constrains the faithful by a clear reason; if you want, he says, to become participants of his resurrection, imitate also the virtue of death, so that dead to vices you may live in virtue; for then you will be partners in that felicity, if you shall have borne the image of his death by dying to sins; for our old human being ought to be taught as fixed to his cross, so that it may destroy the body of sin by the fortitude namely of passion. But Paul by his custom calls the body of sin vices, not the substance of flesh; for so it follows: So that the body of sin may be destroyed, so that we may no longer serve sin; for he who has died has been justified from sin.

lemmas.lexica: LS imitatio; Blaise moral copying vs generation of sin
LS donum; Blaise grace-gift vs inherited sin
LS iustificatio; Blaise forensic making-just, not later system
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin
LS mors; Blaise temporal vs eternal death in Rom 5

pass_b_english: He says that we died to sin at the time when, to receive the gift of forgiveness, we professed our renunciation of the world and all sins. Remembering the gift, we should therefore live in a way that shows we have been buried with Christ and visibly bear his resurrection in holiness. Just as, after rising from the dead, he undergoes no bodily weakness or scourging, so we too should strive to be invulnerable to all sins and vices. ‘For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also share his resurrection, knowing that our old self was crucified with him so that the body of sin might be destroyed, so that we no longer serve sin. For the one who has died has been justified from sin’ (Romans 6:5–7). He binds believers with clear reasoning. If you wish, he says, to share his resurrection, imitate the power of his death too, so that, dead to vices, you may live in virtue. You will share that happiness if you bear the image of his death by dying to sins. Our old self should be shown nailed to his cross, to destroy the body of sin through the courage of suffering. By ‘body of sin,’ according to his customary usage, Paul means vices, not the substance of flesh. For he continues: ‘So that the body of sin might be destroyed, so that we no longer serve sin. For the one who has died has been justified from sin.’

choices.why: Julian's Rom 5:12 reading: sin passes by copying Adam's example, not by generation/seed.
Rom 5 contrast of Adam's offense and Christ's gift; keep gift, not later 'grace system'.
